one_liner: Ruby on the JVM; with invokedynamic it beat CRuby 2.7.7 on 9 of 13 single-threaded shootout programs once warm.
what_it_does: A full Ruby implementation in Java that runs ordinary Ruby source on a JVM (JRE 21+ for current releases), with Ruby threads mapped to JVM threads and no global interpreter lock. It is used as a replacement `ruby` executable or embedded in Java applications, and Ruby code can call Java classes directly. It is not binary-compatible with CRuby: MRI C extensions do not load, so gems need pure-Ruby, FFI or Java-extension variants.
how_it_is_fast: Ruby source is compiled to JRuby's own IR and interpreted; methods that pass a call-count threshold (jit.threshold) are compiled in a background thread to JVM bytecode (ASM), which HotSpot then optimises and inlines like Java. With compile.invokedynamic, call sites, constants and yields are bound through invokedynamic and method handles (invokebinder) with polymorphic inline caches (invokedynamic.maxpoly 6), so HotSpot can inline through Ruby's dynamic dispatch. Regexps use Joni, a Java port of Oniguruma.
when_to_use: Long-running, CPU-bound Ruby processes (servers, workers, batch jobs) where 1.5-2.2 s of JVM startup and JIT warm-up are amortised; object allocation and numeric loops gained most (binarytrees 5.4x, spectralnorm 4.2x, nbody 2.9x over CRuby 2.7.7, derived from page data)
Multi-threaded Ruby that needs real parallelism on many cores (no GIL)
Ruby code that must call Java libraries or run embedded inside a Java application
Teams already running JVM infrastructure (monitoring, GC tuning, deployment) who want to host Ruby on it
when_not_to_use: Short scripts and CLI tools: the shootout's 'Compile T,s' column shows 1.5-2.2 s before the program starts, against 0.2-0.4 s for CRuby
Memory-constrained hosts: JRuby rows peaked at 0.36-2.1 GB (MaxMem) versus 21-169 MB for CRuby 2.7.7 in the same runs
Apps that depend on gems with MRI C extensions, which JRuby does not support
String, IO and regex-heavy work: slower than CRuby 2.7.7 on fasta (26.86 vs 18.19 s), regexdna (9.49 vs 6.25 s) and revcomp (8.78 vs 4.2 s)
If your comparison point is modern CRuby with YJIT: the cited shootout has no YJIT row and uses CRuby 2.7.7 as the baseline

integration.form: JVM runtime (jruby-dist tarball, jruby-complete jar or Maven artifacts for embedding)
integration.dependencies: a JVM (JRE 21+ for current master and 10.x); bundles ASM, Joni, jcodings, invokebinder and jnr-ffi/jffi (core/pom.rb)
integration.min_toolchain: JRE 21 or newer to run current releases; JDK 21+ and Maven wrapper to build (BUILDING.md); the 9.4 line measured here ran on OpenJDK 19
integration.platforms: any OS/CPU with a supported JVM; FFI uses jffi's bundled native stubs
integration.thread_safety: Ruby threads run in parallel on JVM threads with no global interpreter lock (README); thread-safety guarantees of core collections are not documented in the files read
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: runs the same Ruby source (9.4 targets Ruby 3.1.7, master targets Ruby 4.0.0 per default.build.properties) but no MRI C extensions, and startup/memory behaviour differ sharply

gotchas: The invokedynamic default depends on the release: on the 9.4 branch calculateInvokedynamicDefault() returns false, while 10.0 and master set compile.invokedynamic to true; the shootout's JRuby_InDy row is therefore the one that approximates current defaults, and the plain 'JRuby' row (9.4 default, indy off) also loses on matmul (27.1 vs 18.39 s) and nbody (51.32 vs 43.56 s)

Harness asymmetry in kostya/jit-benchmarks: times come from Time.now inside the script, after a 'started' marker, as the best of up to 5 in-process iterations, so JVM boot and most JIT warm-up are excluded; but the stdin-fed programs (knucleotide, regexdna, revcomp) are run with args [1], one cold iteration per process, so two of JRuby's three losses are measured without warm-up, and some rows (CRuby and default JRuby on nbody and brainfuck) completed only 1 iteration inside the timeout
No -Xmx or other JVM heap flags were passed (tools/languages.rb), so the 0.36-2.1 GB MaxMem figures reflect default JVM heap sizing on an 80 GB host; footprint under a capped heap was not measured
The wiki's --dev startup flag turns off the JIT (compile.mode=OFF) and invokedynamic, and the wiki notes the JIT can slow very short runs; benchmark with the same flags you deploy with
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Topaz beat CRuby 2.7.7 on 12 of 13 programs in the same run and was faster than JRuby on most of them, and TruffleRuby's GraalVM rows in that table were faster still (binarytrees 0.69 s vs 1.24 s, mandelbrot 1.34 s vs 7.12 s); pick JRuby when you need an actively maintained Ruby implementation with mature Java interop and real threads rather than the top single-threaded number.
verified_claims_summary: In kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28; AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10), JRuby 9.4.1.0 on OpenJDK 19.0.1 with -Xcompile.invokedynamic=true beat CRuby 2.7.7p221 (built from source with gcc 12.2.0, default flags) on 9 of 13 single-threaded programs, for example binarytrees 1.24 vs 6.75 s and spectralnorm 4.09 vs 17.18 s, using best in-process iteration times that exclude 1.5-2.2 s of JVM startup; it lost on fasta, regexdna and revcomp and roughly tied on matmul.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-03, master is 10.1.3.0-SNAPSHOT) under EPL-2.0/GPL-2.0/LGPL-2.1; usable as a production Ruby runtime, but the cited numbers are for the older 9.4.1.0 release against an end-of-life CRuby 2.7.
